faqs.q: How accurate is this sunrise/sunset calculator?

faqs.a: Two reasons. First, clock time covers a whole timezone, but the Sun peaks at 12:00 only on the zone's central meridian. Second, Earth's orbit is elliptical and its axis is tilted, so the length of a solar day varies through the year — the equation of time shifts solar noon by up to about 16 minutes.
faqs.q: Why is solar noon not at 12:00?

faqs.a: Above the Arctic Circle (and below the Antarctic Circle) the Sun can stay above the horizon for 24 hours in summer — the midnight sun — or below it all winter. When the math detects this, the tool says so instead of inventing times.

faqs.a: Golden hour is roughly the first hour after sunrise and the last hour before sunset, when sunlight is warm and soft — prized by photographers. Blue hour is the twilight just before sunrise and after sunset. This tool's sunrise and sunset times mark their boundaries.

sunrise-sunset-calculator.formula:
NOAA solar algorithm (simplified):
1. Day of year N; longitude hour = longitude / 15
2. Approx time t = N + (6 - lngHour) / 24 for sunrise, N + (18 - lngHour) / 24 for sunset
3. Sun's mean anomaly M = 0.9856 x t - 3.289
4. True longitude L = M + 1.916·sin M + 0.020·sin 2M + 282.634
5. Right ascension RA from L; declination via sinDec = 0.39782·sin L
6. Hour angle: cosH = (cos 90.833° - sinDec·sinLat) / (cosDec·cosLat)
7. Local mean time T = H + RA - 0.06571·t - 6.622; UTC time = T - lngHour

keyFacts: Sunrise and sunset depend on only three things: your latitude, your longitude, and the date.
The tool uses the official zenith angle of 90.833 degrees, which accounts for atmospheric refraction and the Sun's apparent size — this is why its times match published almanacs.
Solar noon is the moment the Sun stands highest. It rarely falls exactly at 12:00 because of your longitude offset and the equation of time.
Near the poles the Sun can stay up (or down) for a full 24 hours — the tool detects polar day and polar night instead of showing fake times.
Times are displayed in your device's timezone. The underlying math is computed in UTC, so daylight-saving changes can never corrupt the result.
